client: I've been really struggling lately with this huge group project I got assigned at university. There's going to be a final presentation in front of the whole class, and just thinking about it makes my chest tight and my mind go blank. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to make the anxiety go away, but I figured I'd at least try.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and giving this a try — it takes courage to reach out even when you're not sure it'll help. I can hear in the pace and tension of your words that this presentation is already weighing heavily on you, stirring up that tight, overwhelming feeling just by thinking about it. What we can work on together is gently exploring the thoughts that are fueling that anxiety, because often it's not the presentation itself but the stories our mind tells us about it that feel so suffocating.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess that makes sense, like intellectually I can follow what you're saying about stories we tell ourselves. But honestly, when I'm standing up there in front of everyone and my mind goes blank, it doesn't feel like a story — it feels completely real and like it's actually happening. I've bombed presentations before, so it's not like I'm just making it up out of nowhere.
therapist: You're absolutely right, and I don't want to dismiss that — past experiences of struggling in presentations are real evidence, and it makes complete sense that your mind holds onto those moments. What I notice is that even as you push back on this, your voice carries something almost careful and tentative, like part of you is still trying to make sense of it all rather than being fully convinced either way. In CBT, we don't ignore that evidence — instead, we look at the *full* picture, asking questions like: were there also moments you got through it, even imperfectly, and what does that tell us too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... yeah, there have been times where I got through a presentation without completely falling apart, but I always just chalked that up to luck or the fact that nobody was really paying attention. It's hard to see those as actual evidence that I can do it, because my brain immediately finds a reason why they don't count. I don't know, maybe I'm just really good at dismissing anything positive before it has a chance to stick.
therapist: You just named something really important — your brain has a built-in system for disqualifying the positive, and you're already aware enough to catch it happening, which is actually a significant insight. I notice you said that quite quickly, almost like the thought rushed out before it could be second-guessed, and yet underneath it there's something that sounds a little deflated, like you're tired of your own mind working against you. That pattern — "it doesn't count because of luck, or because no one cared" — is a classic cognitive distortion called *discounting the positive*, and the fact that you can already see it so clearly means we have something real to work with.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I mean... I guess I can see the pattern when you point it out like that. But knowing it's a distortion doesn't really make it feel any less true in the moment — like, my brain still goes straight to "that doesn't count" even when I'm watching it happen. It's kind of exhausting, honestly, like being a spectator to your own mind sabotaging you and not being able to do anything about it.
therapist: That exhaustion you're describing is so valid — there's something uniquely draining about having the awareness without yet having the ability to intervene, like watching a car skid in slow motion. I notice you're speaking quite quickly, almost like the words are tumbling out under pressure, which makes me wonder if even talking about this pattern is activating that same overwhelmed feeling right now. The good news is that awareness really is the first step — the goal isn't to immediately stop the thought, but to slowly build a little more distance between seeing it and believing it, and that's something we can practice together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that even talking about it is making me feel kind of wound up right now, like my chest is tightening just explaining it. But I guess I'm a bit skeptical about this "distance" thing you're describing, because in the moment it feels like there's no gap at all, it's just instant, like the thought and the panic are the same thing happening at once. How am I supposed to create space when it all happens so fast?
therapist: That high, soft, fast quality in your voice right now actually tells me something important — your body is already demonstrating exactly what you're describing, that quick automatic activation, even here in a safe conversation. Your skepticism makes complete sense, because you're right that in the moment it feels instantaneous, like thought and panic are fused together — but what we're actually trying to build is less like hitting a pause button mid-skid, and more like gradually training your nervous system to recognize the *very earliest* warning signs, like that chest tightening you just noticed, so the gap slowly becomes visible over time. You actually just did a version of it right now by noticing the tightness while it was happening — that's not nothing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I did notice it, yeah, but it feels like such a small thing compared to how fast everything spirals when I'm actually in the middle of it. Like, noticing tightness in my chest here, talking to you, feels manageable, but when it's happening at work and someone's waiting on me to respond and I can feel myself going blank, I don't know how that same skill is supposed to transfer. It just feels like two completely different situations.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched up, like you're already half-bracing for the moment you're describing — actually makes a lot of sense, because your mind is genuinely trying to problem-solve something that feels urgent and unsolved. You're right that a quiet conversation and a high-stakes moment at work feel worlds apart, and I don't want to minimize that gap — but the skill doesn't transfer by being perfect in the hard moment first, it transfers by practicing noticing in the easier moments until it becomes just a little more automatic. Think of it like building a muscle — right now you're lifting something light, and that *is* the training, even when it doesn't feel like enough yet.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about the muscle-building thing, and part of me gets it logically, but I keep coming back to this fear that when my boss is actually staring at me waiting for an answer, all that "noticing" practice is just going to evaporate. Like, it's one thing to catch my breath when I'm alone at home, but the second someone at work looks at me like I'm already failing, my mind just goes completely blank and I freeze up. I guess I'm worried that I'm already too far behind, like everyone else figured this out years ago and I'm just now trying to learn something I should have always known.
therapist: That last part — "something I should have always known" — I want to gently pause there, because your voice is moving very fast and pitched high, like there's a real urgency to get that fear out, and I think it's carrying something deeper than just worry about presentations. There's no age limit on learning to manage anxiety, and the fact that it feels like "everyone else figured this out" is itself one of those stories your mind tells — convincing, but not necessarily true. You're not behind, you're just here now, and that's exactly where this work starts.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like I'm just making excuses for myself. Like, other people manage to stand up and give a presentation without their heart racing out of their chest, so why can't I just... do that? I guess what bothers me most is that I don't even know when this started, it's like the anxiety was always just there, and I've been white-knuckling through every work presentation for years without ever actually dealing with it.
therapist: There's something really significant in what you just shared — your voice is soft and fast, like you're carrying something heavy that you've never quite put down, and the image of "white-knuckling through" for years tells me this has been an exhausting, lonely way to cope. Calling it "making excuses" is actually your inner critic doing what it does best — reframing years of genuine struggle as a character flaw, when really what you're describing is someone who kept showing up despite being in real pain. The fact that you don't know when it started doesn't mean it's permanent or unfixable — it just means it's been there long enough that it feels like *you*, when really it's something that happened *to* you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it's hard not to feel like you're just being kind because that's your job. Like, if it really was something that "happened to me," wouldn't I have some clear memory of a starting point, some event I could point to? The fact that I can't find that just makes me feel like maybe I really am just wired this way, and no amount of reframing is going to change that.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, soft, almost like you're bracing for disappointment — tells me this fear of being "just wired this way" carries a real heaviness, like you're half-expecting me to confirm your worst suspicion about yourself. I want to be honest with you: I'm not saying these things to be kind, I'm saying them because anxiety very often *doesn't* have a single clear origin story, and the absence of one isn't evidence that it's hardwired — it's actually quite common for it to build gradually, quietly, until it just feels like personality. That belief — "this is just who I am" — is often the most important thing we challenge in this work, because it's the one that makes everything else feel pointless, and it deserves a lot of careful, honest attention.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it's hard not to feel like you're just doing your job, you know, like saying the thing you're supposed to say to keep me from giving up. Because honestly, I've felt this way for as long as I can remember, and I can't point to some event or moment where it started, which makes it feel even more like it's just baked into me. I guess I'm scared that if we dig around and don't find anything, that'll actually prove my worst fear right.
therapist: The urgency and intensity in your voice right now — loud, fast, pitched high — tells me this fear isn't abstract, it feels like something is genuinely at stake in this moment, like you're almost testing whether I'll flinch and confirm the worst. I want to gently turn that fear around though: what if finding nothing doesn't prove you're broken, but instead proves that anxiety doesn't always need a dramatic origin to be real and treatable — that it can grow quietly from temperament, environment, small accumulated moments, and still be something that changes? The absence of a "smoking gun" isn't a dead end, it's actually an invitation to work with who you are *now*, rather than searching for a past that explains you away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
